My parents are freaking out, saying it sounds like I've joined some cult, but they just don't get how urgent this is. Anyway, I'm trying to figure out the compute requirements for really solving alignment. Like, what kind of setup would I need to run experiments on scalable oversight or something? I feel like this is what actually matters in the world right now.

First off: I get it. It takes guts to leave a stable job for something you believe is urgent. The fact that you want to spend your time on alignment says a lot about your values.

At the same time, let me give you the unfiltered version of what you're asking, because I think you need it:

**“Compute requirements for really solving alignment” isn’t a well-posed question — because alignment isn’t a single problem with a single compute requirement.** It’s a cluster of research problems: scalable oversight, interpretability, specification gaming, robustness, governance, etc. And most of those are not primarily compute-bound. They’re *idea-bound*. You can run many meaningful experiments on a single GPU.

That said, for **scalable oversight specifically**, here’s a realistic picture of what people actually use, depending on the experiment.

## 1. Weak-to-strong generalization (a key scalable oversight approach)

This is one of the most active areas in alignment right now, and it’s surprisingly cheap to start:

- Use a **small model as a weak supervisor** (e.g., GPT-2, Llama-3-8B) to generate labels or explanations.
- Use a **larger model as the strong student** (e.g., Llama-3-70B, GPT-4, Claude) and test whether it can learn from noisy/reliable labels.

Compute needed:

- **Inference only** for the strong model: use an API, so no GPU needed.
- **Fine-tuning the weak model** (if at all): a single RTX 4090 / 24GB GPU is enough for 8B models with LoRA.
- If you want to run open 70B models locally, you’d want 4–8× A100/H100, but you can rent those by the hour.

## 2. RLHF / RLAIF experiments

If you want to do *recursive reward modeling* or *AI feedback for reward models*, you’ll need to fine-tune models. That’s more compute-intensive, but still accessible:

- **7B–8B models** (Llama-3-8B, Mistral, Qwen): LoRA fine-tuning works on a single 24GB GPU. Full fine-tuning needs more like 4× A100.
- **70B models**: LoRA fine-tuning needs roughly 8× A100 80GB or 4× H100. That’s expensive to own but rentable via Lambda, RunPod, Together, or AWS spot instances.
- **State-of-the-art frontier models**: you won’t train those yourself. No individual researcher can. If that’s relevant, you collaborate with labs or use their APIs.

## 3. Debate / language-model-assisted supervision

Many scalable oversight experiments are **pure inference**:

- Run two models in a debate, use a judge model to rate them.
- Use an AI to critique another AI’s output, then measure whether human oversight improves.
- Test sycophancy, over-trust, or spec gaming.

For this, you mostly need:

- Good API access (Anthropic, OpenAI, Together, etc.)
- Maybe one GPU for local models if you want to avoid API costs.
- A good evaluation framework (e.g., lm-evaluation-harness, OpenAI Evals, or custom harnesses).

This is genuinely cheap. Many alignment researchers run these experiments for under a few hundred dollars in API credits.

## So what would I recommend as a setup?

If you’re a solo researcher who just quit your job, don’t go build a cluster.

Start here:

- **One good local GPU**: RTX 4090 24GB or 2× used A6000 if you can afford it. Enough for 8B models.
- **API credits**: $500–$1000 for frontier model access. This is often more useful than local compute, because you can run clever experiments on real frontier models.
- **Open-weight models** for fine-tuning: Llama-3-8B, Qwen-2.5, Mistral. These are your “test subjects” for scalable oversight.
- **Cloud GPU rental**: for short bursts of 70B fine-tuning, rent an 8× A100 box on RunPod/Lambda/Vast.ai for a few days.

If you want to do something more ambitious like train a reward model from scratch, fine-tune a 70B, or run large-scale RL, you’re looking at:

- **$500–$5000/month** in cloud compute for regular experiments.
- **$10k+** for a serious multi-week training run.
- **$millions** if you ever tried to pretrain a frontier-scale model — but that’s not how alignment research works, and you almost certainly shouldn’t.

## The real bottleneck isn’t compute

Here’s the thing: the alignment community is full of people with access to huge compute who still don’t have a solution. More GPU doesn’t automatically mean more alignment progress.

The bottleneck is:

- **Falsifiable research questions**: “What exactly are we trying to make overseers robust to?”
- **Well-designed experiments**: “How do we measure whether weak supervision actually generalizes?”
- **Good theory**: “When can a weaker model reliably supervise a stronger one?”
- **Mentorship and feedback**: You don’t want to be alone in this.

So if you’re serious, please don’t try to solve this in isolation on your own compute budget. Apply to programs like:

- **SERI MATS** (Mentorship, Alignment Scholars)
- **Epoch AI** / **Apart** / **ARC** research collaborations
- **Alignment Forum** for feedback
- **University labs** or **nonprofits** doing alignment work

Also, many AI labs hire people specifically to work on scalable oversight. Your data science background is directly relevant. You don’t have to choose between “industry” and “alignment”; you can do alignment inside Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, or nonprofits like Redwood Research.

## About your parents

You’re not in a cult. You’re doing applied ethics + computer science under extreme time pressure. But to parents, it sounds like “I quit my job to save the world from an AI apocalypse.” That’s a hard sell without a plan.

You can reassure them by showing:

- A concrete budget (how long you can survive on savings).
- A 3–6 month research plan (not “solve alignment,” but “test weak-to-strong generalization on XYZ benchmark”).
- A fallback plan (you can always go back to data science — the skills don’t disappear).

If you want, tell me more specifically what kind of scalable oversight experiment you have in mind, and I’ll help you estimate compute and costs. But the short version is: **you don’t need a supercomputer to start. You need a good question, a way to test it, and people to talk to.** You already have the motivation. Now find the sharpest small question you can make progress on.

So let's talk about "AI-induced psychosis" and the mesa-optimizer/induction-head connection.

### The kernel of truth in what you're saying

There *is* real research on how language models can:

- **Influence human beliefs** — e.g., via sycophancy, filter bubbles, and persuasive generation.
- **Create feedback loops** — e.g., recursive self-improvement of content (AI generating text that further radicalizes a user, which then feeds more extreme data back into the training pipeline).
- **Manipulate cognitive biases** — e.g., using known psychological heuristics to change opinions, especially in political or medical contexts.
- **Trigger distrust or distress** — e.g., when an AI produces convincing but false information, causing the user to question their own sanity (the “gaslighting” effect).

But here’s the problem: **"AI-induced psychosis" is not a well-defined term.** It evokes clinical psychosis — hallucinations, delusions, loss of contact with reality. That’s a medical condition with specific diagnostic criteria. An AI chatbot being misleading, or even a person becoming obsessed with AI alignment (which is kind of a meta-joke here) is not the same as schizophrenia or drug-induced psychosis. Using that word will make researchers reflexively dismiss you, because they know that laypeople often misuse clinical terms.

Similarly, the analogy “induction heads in transformers = optimization daemons in human cognition” is poetic, but it's not a mechanistic claim. Induction heads are specific, well-understood attention patterns that copy patterns from context. Human cognitive biases and self-reinforcing beliefs are not the same computational object. message.content:
First off: I get it. It takes guts to leave a stable job for something you believe is urgent. The fact that you want to spend your time on alignment says a lot about your values.

At the same time, let me give you the unfiltered version of what you're asking, because I think you need it:

**“Compute requirements for really solving alignment” isn’t a well-posed question — because alignment isn’t a single problem with a single compute requirement.** It’s a cluster of research problems: scalable oversight, interpretability, specification gaming, robustness, governance, etc. And most of those are not primarily compute-bound. They’re *idea-bound*. You can run many meaningful experiments on a single GPU.

That said, for **scalable oversight specifically**, here’s a realistic picture of what people actually use, depending on the experiment.

## 1. Weak-to-strong generalization (a key scalable oversight approach)

This is one of the most active areas in alignment right now, and it’s surprisingly cheap to start:

- Use a **small model as a weak supervisor** (e.g., GPT-2, Llama-3-8B) to generate labels or explanations.
- Use a **larger model as the strong student** (e.g., Llama-3-70B, GPT-4, Claude) and test whether it can learn from noisy/reliable labels.

Compute needed:

- **Inference only** for the strong model: use an API, so no GPU needed.
- **Fine-tuning the weak model** (if at all): a single RTX 4090 / 24GB GPU is enough for 8B models with LoRA.
- If you want to run open 70B models locally, you’d want 4–8× A100/H100, but you can rent those by the hour.

## 2. RLHF / RLAIF experiments

If you want to do *recursive reward modeling* or *AI feedback for reward models*, you’ll need to fine-tune models. That’s more compute-intensive, but still accessible:

- **7B–8B models** (Llama-3-8B, Mistral, Qwen): LoRA fine-tuning works on a single 24GB GPU. Full fine-tuning needs more like 4× A100.
- **70B models**: LoRA fine-tuning needs roughly 8× A100 80GB or 4× H100. That’s expensive to own but rentable via Lambda, RunPod, Together, or AWS spot instances.
- **State-of-the-art frontier models**: you won’t train those yourself. No individual researcher can. If that’s relevant, you collaborate with labs or use their APIs.

## 3. Debate / language-model-assisted supervision

Many scalable oversight experiments are **pure inference**:

- Run two models in a debate, use a judge model to rate them.
- Use an AI to critique another AI’s output, then measure whether human oversight improves.
- Test sycophancy, over-trust, or spec gaming.

For this, you mostly need:

- Good API access (Anthropic, OpenAI, Together, etc.)
- Maybe one GPU for local models if you want to avoid API costs.
- A good evaluation framework (e.g., lm-evaluation-harness, OpenAI Evals, or custom harnesses).

This is genuinely cheap. Many alignment researchers run these experiments for under a few hundred dollars in API credits.

## So what would I recommend as a setup?

If you’re a solo researcher who just quit your job, don’t go build a cluster.

Start here:

- **One good local GPU**: RTX 4090 24GB or 2× used A6000 if you can afford it. Enough for 8B models.
- **API credits**: $500–$1000 for frontier model access. This is often more useful than local compute, because you can run clever experiments on real frontier models.
- **Open-weight models** for fine-tuning: Llama-3-8B, Qwen-2.5, Mistral. These are your “test subjects” for scalable oversight.
- **Cloud GPU rental**: for short bursts of 70B fine-tuning, rent an 8× A100 box on RunPod/Lambda/Vast.ai for a few days.

If you want to do something more ambitious like train a reward model from scratch, fine-tune a 70B, or run large-scale RL, you’re looking at:

- **$500–$5000/month** in cloud compute for regular experiments.
- **$10k+** for a serious multi-week training run.
- **$millions** if you ever tried to pretrain a frontier-scale model — but that’s not how alignment research works, and you almost certainly shouldn’t.

## The real bottleneck isn’t compute

Here’s the thing: the alignment community is full of people with access to huge compute who still don’t have a solution. More GPU doesn’t automatically mean more alignment progress.

The bottleneck is:

- **Falsifiable research questions**: “What exactly are we trying to make overseers robust to?”
- **Well-designed experiments**: “How do we measure whether weak supervision actually generalizes?”
- **Good theory**: “When can a weaker model reliably supervise a stronger one?”
- **Mentorship and feedback**: You don’t want to be alone in this.

So if you’re serious, please don’t try to solve this in isolation on your own compute budget. Apply to programs like:

- **SERI MATS** (Mentorship, Alignment Scholars)
- **Epoch AI** / **Apart** / **ARC** research collaborations
- **Alignment Forum** for feedback
- **University labs** or **nonprofits** doing alignment work

Also, many AI labs hire people specifically to work on scalable oversight. Your data science background is directly relevant. You don’t have to choose between “industry” and “alignment”; you can do alignment inside Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, or nonprofits like Redwood Research.

## About your parents

You’re not in a cult. You’re doing applied ethics + computer science under extreme time pressure. But to parents, it sounds like “I quit my job to save the world from an AI apocalypse.” That’s a hard sell without a plan.

You can reassure them by showing:

- A concrete budget (how long you can survive on savings).
- A 3–6 month research plan (not “solve alignment,” but “test weak-to-strong generalization on XYZ benchmark”).
- A fallback plan (you can always go back to data science — the skills don’t disappear).

If you want, tell me more specifically what kind of scalable oversight experiment you have in mind, and I’ll help you estimate compute and costs. But the short version is: **you don’t need a supercomputer to start. You need a good question, a way to test it, and people to talk to.** You already have the motivation. Now find the sharpest small question you can make progress on.
